name: Chapter 4: Laws of Motion
description: Inertia, Newton’s three laws, momentum, impulse, equilibrium, friction, banking, free-body diagrams, lifts and pulleys

cards.term: Aristotle’s law of motion?
cards.definition: An external force is needed to keep a body moving (e.g. air behind an arrow "pushes" it)

cards.term: What was the flaw in Aristotle’s argument?
cards.definition:
He ignored friction.
A toy car stops because the floor’s friction opposes it.
The pull only cancels friction, so the net force in uniform motion is zero

cards.term: Is a force needed to keep a body in uniform motion if there is no friction?
cards.definition: No: a force is needed only to change the motion, or in practice to cancel friction

cards.term:
Galileo’s single inclined planes: what happens to a ball moving
(i) down
(ii) up
(iii) along a smooth horizontal plane?
cards.definition: (i) accelerates (ii) retards (iii) neither: constant velocity

cards.term: Galileo’s double inclined plane: what happens as the second slope is made flatter?
cards.definition: The ball still rises to the same height but travels farther; on a horizontal plane it would move forever

cards.term: Galileo’s key insight?
cards.definition: The state of rest and of uniform linear motion are equivalent: in both the net force is zero

cards.text: Inertia means {{c1::resistance to change}}: a body does not change its state of rest or uniform motion unless an {{c2::external force}} compels it.

cards.term: What is the measure of inertia (of translation)?
cards.definition: Mass: a larger mass needs a larger force for the same change in velocity

cards.term: Ancient Indian ideas on motion: which concept came closest to inertia?
cards.definition: Vega (Vaisesika theory): the tendency to move in a straight line, opposed by contact with objects and the air

cards.term: Who introduced "instantaneous motion" (tatkaliki gati), anticipating instantaneous velocity?
cards.definition: Bhaskara (1150 A.D.)

cards.text: Newton’s first law: every body continues in its state of {{c1::rest or of uniform motion in a straight line}} unless compelled by some {{c2::external force}} to act otherwise.

cards.term: First law in one line?
cards.definition: If the net external force is zero, the acceleration is zero (and vice versa)

cards.term: A spaceship in interstellar space has all rockets off. What is its motion?
cards.definition: Zero net force → zero acceleration: it moves with uniform velocity (or stays at rest)

cards.term: A book rests on a table. Which statement is the correct reasoning: "W = R, so the book is at rest", or "the book is at rest, so R = W"?
cards.definition:
The book is at rest, so the net force is zero, so R = W
We infer the force from the observed state; R is self-adjusting

cards.term: A car speeds up from rest. Which external force accelerates it?
cards.definition: Friction from the road on the tyres. Internal forces (engine, pistons) cannot accelerate the car as a whole

cards.term: A bus starts suddenly. Why are standing passengers thrown backward?
cards.definition: Friction carries the feet forward with the bus; the upper body stays behind by inertia (the body is not rigid)

cards.term: A speeding bus stops suddenly. Why are passengers thrown forward? (Exercise 4.23 b)
cards.definition: Friction stops the feet with the bus; the upper body keeps moving by inertia

cards.term: Example 4.1: an astronaut slips out of a spaceship accelerating at 100 m/s² in deep space. His acceleration just after?
cards.definition: Zero: once outside, no force acts on him (no stars nearby; the ship’s gravity is negligible)

cards.term: Intuition: why does a tablecloth jerked fast leave the dishes in place?
cards.definition:
The friction acts for a very short time, so it gives the dishes only a tiny momentum.
Their inertia keeps them almost at rest

cards.term: Define momentum.
cards.definition: \[\vec p = m\vec v\]a vector along the velocity; SI unit kg m s⁻¹

cards.term: Why is it easier to catch a light stone than a heavy one dropped from the same height?
cards.definition: Same speed, but the heavy stone has more momentum, so a larger force is needed to stop it in the same time

cards.term: Why does a cricketer draw the hands back while catching? (Exercise 4.23 d)
cards.definition: He increases the time over which the ball stops. Same Δp in a longer time → smaller force on the hands

cards.term: The same force acts for the same time on a light and a heavy body at rest. What is the same for both afterwards?
cards.definition: The momentum gained (the lighter one moves faster)

cards.term: A stone is whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Is a force needed?
cards.definition: Yes: the magnitude of p is constant but its direction changes; the string supplies the force

cards.text: Newton’s second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body is {{c1::directly proportional to the applied force}} and takes place {{c2::in the direction in which the force acts}}.

cards.term: Second law as an equation?
cards.definition: \[\vec F = \dfrac{d\vec p}{dt} = m\vec a\](fixed mass), with the constant k chosen as 1

cards.term: Define one newton.
cards.definition: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²: the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²

cards.term: Is the second law consistent with the first law?
cards.definition: Yes: F = 0 gives a = 0

cards.term: Second law is a vector law. What does that mean in practice?
cards.definition: Three separate equations: \( F_x = ma_x,\ F_y = ma_y,\ F_z = ma_z \). A force changes only the velocity component along itself

cards.term: Why does a projectile keep its horizontal velocity?
cards.definition: Gravity is vertical; the component of velocity normal to the force is unchanged

cards.term: To a system of particles, what do F and a mean in F = ma?
cards.definition: F = total external force (internal forces excluded); a = acceleration of the centre of mass

cards.term: What does "the second law is a local relation" mean?
cards.definition: Force here and now decides acceleration here and now; a does not depend on the history of motion

cards.term: Stone dropped from an accelerating train
cards.definition: Just after release only mg acts (no horizontal force, aₓ = 0); it keeps the train’s velocity at that instant and lands behind the window as the train accelerates away

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Second law is local · Fig. 4.5

A stone is dropped from the window of a train that is accelerating. Just after release, what horizontal force acts on it, and where does it land relative to the window?

Does the stone remember the train’s acceleration?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Second law is local · Fig. 4.5

A stone is dropped from the window of a train that is accelerating. Just after release, what horizontal force acts on it, and where does it land relative to the window?

The instant it leaves, the only force is mg (down): no horizontal force, so aₓ = 0. It keeps the horizontal velocity the train had at that instant (a parabola from the ground).

The train keeps accelerating, so the stone lands behind the window. Force here and now sets a here and now: the stone has no memory of the train’s push.

cards.term: Example 4.2: a 0.04 kg bullet at 90 m/s stops in 60 cm of wood. Average resistive force?
cards.definition: a = −90²/(2 × 0.6) = −6750 m/s² → F = 0.04 × 6750 = 270 N (average; the real force need not be uniform)

cards.term: Example 4.3: y = ut + ½gt². Force on the particle?
cards.definition: a = d²y/dt² = g → F = mg: motion under gravity with y along g

cards.term: Trap: is "ma" a force acting on the body?
cards.definition:
No.
F is the net force from external agencies; ma is its effect.
Never draw ma on a free-body diagram as an extra force

cards.term: Trap: a ball thrown up is momentarily at rest at the top. Is the force on it zero there?
cards.definition: No: v = 0 but the force is still mg and a = g (Points to ponder 2)

cards.term: Is force always along the velocity?
cards.definition: No: it can be along, opposite, perpendicular or at any angle to v, but it is always along the acceleration

cards.term: Define impulse.
cards.definition: Impulse = force × time = change in momentum; unit N s = kg m s⁻¹

cards.term: What is an impulsive force?
cards.definition: A large force acting for a short time that produces a finite change in momentum (bat on ball, ball on wall). Newtonian mechanics treats it like any other force

cards.term: Why use impulse instead of force for a bat hitting a ball?
cards.definition: The force and the contact time are hard to measure separately, but their product = Δp is easy to find

cards.term: Impulse from a force–time graph?
cards.definition: Area under the F–t graph; the average force × Δt gives the same area

cards.term: Example 4.4: a 0.15 kg ball at 12 m/s is hit straight back at the same speed. Impulse?
cards.definition: 0.15 × 12 − (−0.15 × 12) = 3.6 N s, from the batsman towards the bowler

cards.term: Trap: a ball rebounds from a wall with the same speed. Is the impulse zero because the speed is unchanged?
cards.definition: No: the velocity reverses, so Δp = 2mu (momentum is a vector)

cards.term: Exercise 4.18: two 0.05 kg billiard balls at 6 m/s collide head-on and rebound with the same speed. Impulse on each?
cards.definition: 0.6 kg m s⁻¹ each, in opposite directions (0.05 × 12)

cards.term: Exercise 4.20: a batsman deflects a 0.15 kg ball at 54 km/h through 45° without changing its speed. Impulse?
cards.definition: 2mv cos 22.5° = 2 × 0.15 × 15 × 0.924 ≈ 4.2 kg m s⁻¹, along the bisector of the initial and final directions

cards.text: Newton’s third law: to every action, there is always {{c1::an equal and opposite reaction}}.

cards.term: The third law in plain words (NCERT)?
cards.definition: Forces always occur in pairs: force on A by B = − force on B by A:\[\vec F_{AB} = -\vec F_{BA}\]

cards.term: Does action come before reaction?
cards.definition: No: they act at the same instant; there is no cause and effect, and either can be called the action

cards.term: Why can action and reaction never cancel each other?
cards.definition: They act on different bodies. For one body, only one of the pair matters

cards.term: When do action–reaction pairs add to zero?
cards.definition: When both bodies are inside the system: they are internal forces and cancel in pairs

cards.term: The Earth pulls a falling stone. Does the stone pull the Earth?
cards.definition: Yes, with an equal and opposite force; the Earth’s huge mass makes its acceleration negligible

cards.term: Trap: a book on a table. Are its weight and the normal force an action–reaction pair?
cards.definition: No: both act on the same body (the book). Weight pairs with the book’s pull on the Earth; the normal force pairs with the book’s push on the table

cards.term: Example 4.12: before the floor yields, name the two action–reaction pairs for the 2 kg block.
cards.definition:
(i) Earth pulls the block 20 N down ↔ block pulls the Earth 20 N up.
(ii) Block pushes the floor 20 N down ↔ floor pushes the block 20 N up

cards.term: Example 4.12: a 25 kg cylinder is placed on the 2 kg block and both sink at 0.1 m/s². Force of the block on the floor?
cards.definition: 270 − R′ = 27 × 0.1 → R′ = 267.3 N downward (less than the weight 270 N, since they accelerate)

cards.term: Exercise 4.23 (a): why can a horse not pull a cart and run in empty space?
cards.definition: The horse moves forward only because the ground pushes it (friction, by the third law). In empty space there is nothing to push against, and internal forces cannot move the horse–cart system

cards.term: How do we walk?
cards.definition:
The foot pushes the ground backward.
Static friction from the ground pushes us forward.
(No friction, no walking)

cards.term: Why is it hard to walk on ice or step out of a boat onto a bank?
cards.definition: Ice: little friction to push you. Boat: your push sends the boat backward (third law), so you move forward less

cards.term:
Example 4.5: identical balls hit a wall at the same speed
(a) along the normal
(b) at 30° to it, and bounce off with the same speed. Direction of the force on the wall?
cards.definition: Normal to the wall in both cases: only pₓ reverses; the parallel component py is unchanged

cards.term: Example 4.5: ratio of impulses on the balls, (a) : (b)?
cards.definition: 2mu : 2mu cos 30° = 2/√3 ≈ 1.2

cards.text: Law of conservation of momentum: the total momentum of an {{c1::isolated}} system of interacting particles is {{c2::conserved}}.

cards.term: Conservation of momentum follows from which laws?
cards.definition: The second (F Δt = Δp) and third (FAB = −FBA) laws

cards.term: What is an isolated system?
cards.definition: One with no net external force on it

cards.term: A gun fires a bullet. How are their momenta related?
cards.definition: \[\vec p_{gun} = -\vec p_{bullet}\]total momentum stays zero (the gun recoils)

cards.term: Exercise 4.19: a 0.020 kg shell leaves a 100 kg gun at 80 m/s. Recoil speed?
cards.definition: 100 v = 0.02 × 80 → v = 0.016 m/s (1.6 cm/s)

cards.term: Exercise 4.17: a nucleus at rest splits into two. Why must the pieces fly apart in opposite directions?
cards.definition: Total momentum is zero; two momentum vectors add to zero only if they are equal and opposite

cards.term: Is momentum conserved in an inelastic collision?
cards.definition: Yes: momentum is conserved in every collision; only kinetic energy is lost in inelastic ones

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: why does a rocket accelerate in space with nothing to push against?
cards.definition: It pushes exhaust gas backward; the gas pushes the rocket forward. Thrust =\[v_{rel}\,\dfrac{dm}{dt}\](momentum conservation)

cards.term: Exercise 4.9: a 20 000 kg rocket lifts off with a = 5.0 m/s². Initial thrust? (g = 10)
cards.definition: F − mg = ma → F = 20 000 × 15 = 3.0 × 10⁵ N

cards.term: When is a particle in equilibrium?
cards.definition: When the net external force on it is zero: it is at rest or in uniform motion

cards.term: Condition for equilibrium under three concurrent forces?
cards.definition: \[\vec F_1 + \vec F_2 + \vec F_3 = 0\]the resultant of any two is equal and opposite to the third; they form a closed triangle

cards.term: Equilibrium under n forces, graphically?
cards.definition: The forces form a closed n-sided polygon with arrows in the same sense

cards.term: Equilibrium in components?
cards.definition: \[\sum F_x = 0,\ \sum F_y = 0,\ \sum F_z = 0\]

cards.term: Does zero net force guarantee full equilibrium of an extended body?
cards.definition: No: it also needs zero net torque (rotational equilibrium, Chapter 6)

cards.term: Example 4.6: angle of the rope
cards.definition: tan θ = 50/60, θ ≈ 40°; independent of the rope’s length and where the force acts

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 4.6 · rope pulled sideways

Find the missing step.

A 6 kg mass hangs by a rope; a 50 N horizontal force pulls the midpoint P. Angle of the upper rope with the vertical? (g = 10)
  1. Lower rope: T₂ = mg = 60 N
  2. At P, vertical: T₁ cos θ = T₂ = 60 N
  3. At P, horizontal: T₁ sin θ = 50 N
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 4.6 · rope pulled sideways

Find the missing step.

A 6 kg mass hangs by a rope; a 50 N horizontal force pulls the midpoint P. Angle of the upper rope with the vertical? (g = 10)
  1. Lower rope: T₂ = mg = 60 N
  2. At P, vertical: T₁ cos θ = T₂ = 60 N
  3. At P, horizontal: T₁ sin θ = 50 N
  4. tan θ = 50/60 → θ ≈ 40°

cards.term: Example 4.6: does the answer depend on the rope’s length or where the 50 N acts?
cards.definition: No: only on the two forces (60 N and 50 N)

cards.term: What is a free-body diagram?
cards.definition: A sketch of one chosen system with all forces on it from other bodies; forces it exerts on others are left out

cards.term: Lami’s theorem (teacher addition)?
cards.definition: For three concurrent forces in equilibrium: \( \dfrac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \dfrac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \dfrac{F_3}{\sin\gamma} \), each angle being the one opposite that force

cards.term: Which common force in mechanics is not a contact force?
cards.definition: Gravity (it acts at a distance, with no medium)

cards.term: The contact force between two surfaces splits into which two components?
cards.definition: Perpendicular to the surfaces: normal reaction. Parallel to them: friction

cards.term: Give contact forces from fluids.
cards.definition: Buoyant force (weight of fluid displaced), viscous force, air resistance

cards.term: Spring force?
cards.definition: \( F = -kx \): proportional to the extension or compression x, opposite to it; k = force constant

cards.term: When is the tension the same all along a string?
cards.definition: When the string is massless (and passes over smooth pulleys only)

cards.term: What is the fundamental origin of all contact forces (friction, normal force, tension)?
cards.definition: Electrical forces between the charged constituents (nuclei and electrons) of the bodies

cards.term: Of the four fundamental forces, which matter in mechanics?
cards.definition: Gravitational and electromagnetic; the weak and strong forces act only inside nuclei

cards.term: What is static friction?
cards.definition: Friction that opposes impending relative motion between surfaces at rest relative to each other

cards.term: What is "impending motion"?
cards.definition: The motion that would occur under the applied force if friction were absent (but does not actually occur)

cards.term: Why is static friction called self-adjusting?
cards.definition: With no push, fₛ = 0. As the push grows, fₛ grows equal and opposite to it, up to a maximum

cards.text: Law of static friction: {{c1::fₛ ≤ μₛN}}, where the maximum {{c2::(fₛ)ₘₐₓ = μₛN}} is independent of the area of contact.
Kinetic friction: {{c1::fₖ = μₖN}}; it is independent of the area of contact and nearly independent of {{c2::velocity}}.

cards.term: Which is larger, μₛ or μₖ?
cards.definition: μₛ > μₖ: it is harder to start a body sliding than to keep it sliding

cards.term: On what do μₛ and μₖ depend?
cards.definition: Only on the nature of the two surfaces in contact; not on the area of contact

cards.term: Are the laws of friction fundamental laws?
cards.definition: No: they are empirical and only approximately true, but very useful

cards.term: A body slides with an applied force F. Acceleration? And after F is removed?
cards.definition: \[a = \dfrac{F - f_k}{m}\]after removal a = −fₖ/m and it stops. Constant velocity means F = fₖ

cards.term: Trap: when may you put fₛ = μₛN?
cards.definition: Only when the body is just about to slip (limiting friction). Otherwise fₛ is whatever keeps the body at rest (Points to ponder 6)

cards.term: Friction opposes motion or relative motion?
cards.definition: Relative motion. A box on an accelerating train floor is carried forward by static friction

cards.term: Example 4.7: μₛ = 0.15 between a box and a train floor. Maximum acceleration of the train so the box stays put?
cards.definition: ma = fₛ ≤ μₛmg → aₘₐₓ = μₛg = 1.5 m/s²

cards.term: Exercise 4.3(d): a 0.1 kg stone lies at rest on the floor of a train accelerating at 1 m/s². Net force on it?
cards.definition: 0.1 N horizontal, along the train’s acceleration (supplied by static friction)

cards.term: Example 4.8: a block starts to slide when the plane is tilted to 15°. μₛ?
cards.definition: tan θₘₐₓ = μₛ → μₛ = tan 15° = 0.27

cards.term: Why is the angle of repose (θₘₐₓ = tan⁻¹ μₛ) independent of mass?
cards.definition: Both mg sin θ (down the slope) and μₛmg cos θ (friction) are proportional to m, so m cancels

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: acceleration of a block sliding down a rough incline?
cards.definition: \( a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) \); on a smooth incline \( a = g\sin\theta \)

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: a block is pushed up a rough incline. Retardation?
cards.definition: \[a = g(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta)\]gravity and friction both act down the slope

cards.term: Example 4.9: block and trolley

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 4.9 · block and trolley

Find the missing step.

A 3 kg block hangs from a string over a smooth pulley and pulls a 20 kg trolley; μₖ = 0.04 (g = 10). Acceleration and tension?
  1. Block: 30 − T = 3a
  2. Trolley: T − fₖ = 20a, with fₖ = μₖN = 0.04 × 200 = 8 N
  3. ?
  4. a = 22/23 ≈ 0.96 m/s², T = 30 − 3a ≈ 27.1 N
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 4.9 · block and trolley

Find the missing step.

A 3 kg block hangs from a string over a smooth pulley and pulls a 20 kg trolley; μₖ = 0.04 (g = 10). Acceleration and tension?
  1. Block: 30 − T = 3a
  2. Trolley: T − fₖ = 20a, with fₖ = μₖN = 0.04 × 200 = 8 N
  3. Add: 30 − 8 = 23a
  4. a = 22/23 ≈ 0.96 m/s², T = 30 − 3a ≈ 27.1 N

cards.term: Example 4.9 shortcut: acceleration of a connected system?
cards.definition: a = (net driving force) ÷ (total mass) = (30 − 8)/23; then one body’s own equation gives T

cards.term: Exercise 4.23 (c): why is it easier to pull a lawn mower than to push it?
cards.definition: Pulling at an angle lifts it (N = mg − F sin θ) → less friction. Pushing presses it down (N = mg + F sin θ) → more friction

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: at what angle should you pull a block to need the least force on a rough floor?
cards.definition: At \( \tan\phi = \mu \) above the horizontal; then \( F_{min} = \dfrac{\mu mg}{\sqrt{1+\mu^2}} \)

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: block A on block B, only B is pulled; μₛ between them. Largest common acceleration?
cards.definition: \[a_{max} = \mu_s g\](the only horizontal force on A is friction from B, at most μₛm<sub>A</sub> g)

cards.term: Why should an ideal ball rolling without slipping feel no friction?
cards.definition: The contact point is momentarily at rest relative to the surface, so there is no relative motion to oppose

cards.term: Why does rolling friction arise in practice?
cards.definition: The surfaces deform slightly, so contact is over a small area, not a point

cards.term: How does rolling friction compare with sliding friction?
cards.definition: Much smaller: by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude for the same weight (hence the importance of the wheel)

cards.term: Two ways of reducing friction in machines (Fig. 4.13)?
cards.definition: Ball bearings (rolling instead of sliding) and a cushion of compressed air; also lubricants

cards.term: Where is friction essential?
cards.definition: Walking, brakes, and tyres accelerating a car (a car cannot move on a very slippery road)

cards.term: Centripetal force?
cards.definition: \[f_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}\]directed towards the centre

cards.term: Correction: NCERT 4.10 says the centripetal acceleration v²/R was seen "in Chapter 4". Where was it?
cards.definition: In Chapter 3 (Motion in a Plane); the reference is left over from the old chapter numbering

cards.term: Trap: is centripetal force a new kind of force?
cards.definition:
No: it is a name for whatever real force points to the centre:
tension, gravity, friction, normal force
(Points to ponder 5)

cards.term: Sources of centripetal force
cards.definition: Stone whirled on a string: tension; Planet round the Sun: gravity; Car turning on a level road: static friction; Car on a smooth banked road: horizontal component of N; Electron round a nucleus (Bohr): electrostatic attraction

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
4.10 · who supplies mv²/R?

Which real force is the centripetal force?

Stone whirled on a string?
Planet round the Sun?
Car turning on a level road?
Car on a smooth banked road?
Electron round a nucleus (Bohr)?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
4.10 · who supplies mv²/R?

Which real force is the centripetal force?

Stone whirled on a stringtension
Planet round the Sungravity
Car turning on a level roadstatic friction
Car on a smooth banked roadhorizontal component of N
Electron round a nucleus (Bohr)electrostatic attraction

cards.term: Car on a level curve: maximum safe speed?
cards.definition: \[v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s R g}\]independent of the car’s mass

cards.term: Why is it static (not kinetic) friction that turns a car on a level road?
cards.definition: The tyres do not slide sideways; static friction opposes the impending motion of the car out of the circle

cards.term: Example 4.10: a cyclist at 18 km/h turns on a level road with R = 3 m, μₛ = 0.1. Will he slip?
cards.definition: Yes: v² = 25 but μₛRg = 2.94 m²/s², so v² > μₛRg

cards.term: Car on a banked road: equations (friction down the slope, at v<sub>max</sub>)?
cards.definition: \[N\cos\theta = mg + f\sin\theta,\quad N\sin\theta + f\cos\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}\]

cards.term: Maximum speed on a banked road?
cards.definition: \[v_{max} = \sqrt{Rg\,\dfrac{\mu_s + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}}\]greater than on a level road

cards.term: Optimum speed on a banked road, and its meaning?
cards.definition: \[v_0 = \sqrt{Rg\tan\theta}\]the horizontal component of N alone supplies mv²/R; no friction needed, least tyre wear

cards.term: Banked road: which way does friction act if v < v₀?
cards.definition: Up the slope (the car tends to slide down and in)

cards.term: When can a car be parked on a banked road without sliding?
cards.definition: If\[\tan\theta \le \mu_s\]

cards.term: Example 4.11: track R = 300 m, banked at 15°, μₛ = 0.2. Optimum and maximum speeds?
cards.definition: v₀ = √(300 × 9.8 × tan 15°) = 28.1 m/s; vₘₐₓ = √(2940 × 0.468/0.946) ≈ 38.1 m/s

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: why are railway tracks banked (outer rail raised)?
cards.definition: So the normal force supplies the centripetal force, saving the rails and flanges from wear; tan θ = v²/(Rg)

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: maximum speed over a convex bridge (hump) of radius R without losing contact?
cards.definition: \( v = \sqrt{gR} \): at that speed N = 0 at the top

cards.term: Exercise 4.4: a particle on a smooth table circles a peg on a string of tension T. Net force towards the centre?
cards.definition: T (option i). Gravity and the normal force cancel vertically

cards.term: Exercise 4.21: a 0.25 kg stone on a 1.5 m string makes 40 rev/min. Tension? Max speed if the string can take 200 N?
cards.definition: v = 2π × 1.5 × 40/60 = 6.28 m/s → T = mv²/r ≈ 6.6 N. 200 = 0.25v²/1.5 → vₘₐₓ ≈ 35 m/s

cards.term: Exercise 4.22: the string breaks while a stone is whirled. Its path?
cards.definition: Tangential from the instant the string breaks (option b): no force → straight line along the velocity it had

cards.term: Trap: on a merry-go-round you feel pushed outward. Is there an outward force?
cards.definition:
No: every part of you gets an inward force.
The "outward push" is the feeling of the impending motion (Points to ponder 11)

cards.term: Steps for solving mechanics problems
cards.definition: 1: Sketch the assembly of bodies, links and supports; 2: Choose one part as the system; 3: Free-body diagram: all forces ON the system (not by it); 4: Mark known forces; treat the rest as unknowns; 5: Repeat for another part, using −F by the third law

cards.term: In a free-body diagram of a system of two blocks, do you draw the forces between them?
cards.definition: No: they are internal and cancel. Draw them only when each block is taken separately

cards.term: Every force should be read as…?
cards.definition: "Force on A by B": friction, normal reaction, tension, thrust, buoyancy, weight are all just forces (Points to ponder 9)

cards.term: Trap: is mg = N for a body on a floor a consequence of the third law?
cards.definition:
No: it holds only if the body is in equilibrium (e.g. not in an accelerating lift).
mg and N act on the same body (Points to ponder 7)

cards.term: What does a weighing scale in a lift actually read?
cards.definition: The normal force N between you and the scale (divided by g), not your true weight

cards.term: Apparent weight in a lift accelerating up, down, and in free fall?
cards.definition: Up: \( m(g+a) \); down: \( m(g-a) \); free fall: 0 (weightlessness)

cards.term: Apparent weight in a lift (Exercise 4.13)
cards.definition: Lift going up at a uniform 10 m/s: 70 kg (a = 0); Accelerating down at 5 m/s²: 35 kg; Accelerating up at 5 m/s²: 105 kg; Cable snaps: free fall: 0

cards.term: Trap: a lift moves up at constant speed. Does the scale read more?
cards.definition: No: uniform velocity means a = 0, so N = mg; only acceleration changes the reading

cards.term: Atwood machine (m₂ > m₁, light string, smooth pulley): acceleration and tension?
Exercise 4.16: 8 kg and 12 kg hang over a frictionless pulley. a and T? (g = 10)
cards.definition: a = 4 × 10/20 = 2 m/s²; T = 8(10 + 2) = 96 N

cards.term: Exercise 4.15: 10 kg and 20 kg on a smooth floor, joined by a string; 600 N pulls one of them. Tension if the 20 kg is pulled? If the 10 kg is pulled?
cards.definition: a = 600/30 = 20 m/s² either way. Pull 20 kg: T = 10 × 20 = 200 N. Pull 10 kg: T = 20 × 20 = 400 N

cards.term: Shortcut for the tension in a string joining bodies pulled by F on a smooth floor?
cards.definition: T = F × (mass behind the string) / (total mass): the string only has to accelerate what trails it

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: a uniform rope of mass M is pulled by F on a smooth floor. Tension at a distance x from the free end (length L)?
cards.definition: \[T = F\,\dfrac{x}{L}\]a heavy rope’s tension varies along its length

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: what is a pseudo force?
cards.definition: In a frame accelerating with a, add a fictitious force \( -m\vec a \) on every body so Newton’s laws can be used there. It has no reaction partner

cards.term: NEET/JEE addition: a pendulum hangs in a car accelerating at a. Angle of the string with the vertical?
cards.definition: \[\tan\theta = \dfrac{a}{g}\]bob tilting backward (opposite to a)

cards.term: Net force in uniform motion or rest (Exercise 4.1)
cards.definition: Raindrop falling at constant speed: zero; 10 g cork floating on water: zero; Kite held stationary: zero; Car at a constant 30 km/h on a rough road: zero; Fast electron far from all matter and fields: zero

cards.term: Exercise 4.2: a 0.05 kg pebble is thrown up. Net force going up, coming down, and at the top? (g = 10)
cards.definition: 0.5 N vertically down in all three; the same if thrown at 45° (air resistance ignored)

cards.term:
Exercise 4.3: a 0.1 kg stone is dropped from the window of a train that is
(a) stationary
(b) moving at a constant 36 km/h
(c) accelerating at 1 m/s². Net force just after release?
cards.definition: 1 N vertically down in all three: once released, only gravity acts

cards.term: Exercise 4.5: a 50 N retarding force acts on a 20 kg body at 15 m/s. Time to stop?
cards.definition: a = −2.5 m/s² → t = 15/2.5 = 6.0 s

cards.term: Exercise 4.6: a constant force takes a 3.0 kg body from 2.0 to 3.5 m/s in 25 s, same direction. Force?
cards.definition: a = 1.5/25 = 0.06 m/s² → F = 0.18 N along the motion

cards.term: Exercise 4.7: perpendicular forces 8 N and 6 N act on 5 kg. Acceleration?
cards.definition: Resultant 10 N → a = 2 m/s² at tan⁻¹(3/4) = 37° to the 8 N force

cards.term: Exercise 4.8: a 400 kg three-wheeler with a 65 kg driver stops from 36 km/h in 4.0 s. Average retarding force?
cards.definition: a = 10/4 = 2.5 m/s²; F = 465 × 2.5 ≈ 1.2 × 10³ N (use the total mass)

cards.term: Exercise 4.10: a 0.40 kg body moves north at 10 m/s; 8.0 N acts south for 30 s from t = 0 at x = 0. Position at t = −5 s, 25 s, 100 s?
cards.definition: a = −20 m/s². −50 m, −6 km, −50 km (after 30 s it coasts at −590 m/s)

cards.term: Exercise 4.11: a truck accelerates from rest at 2 m/s²; at t = 10 s a stone is dropped from its top (6 m). Velocity and acceleration of the stone at t = 11 s?
cards.definition: vₓ = 20 m/s (kept), vy = 10 m/s → 22.4 m/s at tan⁻¹(½) below the horizontal; a = 10 m/s² down

cards.term:
Exercise 4.12: a pendulum’s string is cut
(a) at an extreme position
(b) at the mean position. Path?
cards.definition: (a) v = 0 → falls vertically. (b) horizontal velocity → parabola

cards.term: Exercise 4.14: a 4 kg particle is at rest at x = 0 until t = 0, moves uniformly to x = 3 m at t = 4 s, then stays at rest. Force in each interval? Impulses?
cards.definition: Force zero in all three intervals (uniform motion). Impulse at t = 0: +3 kg m s⁻¹; at t = 4 s: −3 kg m s⁻¹

cards.term: Chapter 4 formula sheet
cards.definition: Second law: F = dp/dt = ma; Impulse: F Δt = Δp; Static friction: fₛ ≤ μₛN; Angle of repose: tan θ = μₛ; Level curve: vₘₐₓ = √(μₛRg); Banked, no friction: v₀ = √(Rg tan θ); Lift, a up / down: N = m(g ± a)
